individual_teacher_note: Liquids and gases flow and are fluids. This is foundational vocabulary; the B-35 official outcome emphasizes defining/applying steady, incompressible and non-viscous IDEAL flow, so foundational item-level board alignment remains pending.

scientific_theme: Volumetric flow rate is supporting practice
individual_teacher_note: Q=V/t means volume crossing a point or cross-section per unit time, so source A is right. However the official P-11-B-35 wording does NOT explicitly require volume-per-time formula calculations. Preserve as extra learning practice but do not individually certify as a B-35 board question without separate SLO evaluation.

The prepared section introduces orderly streamline and disordered turbulent flow. Original NBF printed pp.95–96 were not reopened to certify exact two-category attribution, although the teacher source key D is supported.
Smooth paths capture the intended teacher textbook model. In wider fluid mechanics, streamline geometry and particle pathlines coincide in steady flow; they need not be identical for unsteady flow.

scientific_theme: Steady means unchanged velocity at each fixed location, not uniform everywhere
individual_teacher_note: A STEADY velocity field has ∂v/∂t=0 at a fixed spatial location, so successive particles passing that point share the same local velocity. Distinguish this from spatially uniform speed everywhere and from strictly laminar flow; the source D is supported under its stated steady assumption.

scientific_theme: Streamlines do not intersect in well-defined velocity field
individual_teacher_note: Two streamlines cannot geometrically cross at a point with a unique, nonzero local velocity direction; streamline directions can be indeterminate at stagnation points, which is beyond this introductory question.

scientific_theme: Steady and laminar are not universal synonyms
individual_teacher_note: The prepared NBF-based introduction associates smooth streamline flow with laminar flow, so source B matches its wording. In general, steady (unchanging in time at a location) and laminar (ordered layered regime) are DIFFERENT flow properties. Avoid teaching them as unconditional synonyms; verify exact printed NBF phrasing separately.

scientific_theme: Centerline faster only with specified tube flow conditions
individual_teacher_note: Middle layers are generally faster than near-wall layers in pressure-driven laminar pipe flow with no-slip walls and an established profile. This is not universal for every laminar tube flow, e.g. plug-like moving-wall flow; keep source A as introductory model result with conditions explained.

scientific_theme: Laminar regime depends on Reynolds conditions
individual_teacher_note: Lower speeds often favor laminar motion when fluid viscosity, density, conduit dimension and disturbances are otherwise comparable. It is Reynolds number/flow geometry, not absolute speed alone, that governs onset of turbulence.
Irregular time-varying vortical eddies distinguish a turbulent regime from a smooth laminar one; original C scientifically supported.
Eddy is a local swirling feature of fluid motion; it is common in turbulent flow, although existence of a vortex alone does not universally establish turbulence.

scientific_theme: Critical speed is setup-dependent and transition may vary
individual_teacher_note: The source D captures an introductory threshold description, but critical flow speed is NOT a universal fixed number. Transition depends on Reynolds number, flow geometry, disturbance level and fluid properties. A threshold is not guaranteed to be sharp for all configurations.
A smooth streamlined shape often reduces flow separation and drag for suitable orientation and Reynolds conditions, but is not a guarantee of laminar or drag-free flow.
Non-viscous/inviscid model neglects viscosity-generated internal tangential friction; density and pressure may still be nonzero.

At this textbook level incompressible flow means fluid density is modeled constant; it does not require zero pressure or equal velocity at all points. More general fluid theory can distinguish material density conservation from spatial homogeneity.
Liquid water is far less compressible than common gases under ordinary conditions, though real water has small but nonzero compressibility.
Source C correctly identifies inviscid flow as an ideal-fluid assumption, which is not the same as absence of all pressure forces.
Source D identifies the intended constant-density idealization, but incompressibility by itself need not entail zero viscosity or steady state.
Real fluids exhibit some viscous shear resistance; ideal inviscid flow is a simplified mathematical model.

scientific_theme: Flow-rate unit m³/s supplementary to B-35
individual_teacher_note: Volumetric flow rate Q=V/t has SI unit m³/s, so C is right. It is source-backed prerequisite knowledge but not explicitly one of the three definitions the official P-11-B-35 outcome names; keep as supporting practice until individual official scope decision.
